title: Does Online Education Suck? A Research Perspective
author: Alfred Essa
summary: Essa reviews a quasi-experimental study (Ortagus, Hughes and Allchin) finding that students in exclusively online degree programs are 8.3 percentage points less likely to complete a bachelor's degree, and the authors' call for tighter regulation. He applies a Tukey-style exploratory mindset and asks for simpler alternative explanations before accepting a causal claim. He first points to an asymmetry in scrutiny: traditional lecture-based programs face little demand for evidence despite the learning-science case against passive instruction. He then critiques the study design: treating 'online' as a single uniform treatment, a 10-to-1 group imbalance, and a heterogeneous control group. His central move is a thought experiment showing that the mix of institution types, especially for-profit colleges, could by itself reproduce the completion gap. He concludes that the policy recommendations may target delivery mode when institutional quality and student circumstances are the real drivers.
points: Essa argues the headline 8.3-point completion gap may reflect which institutions online students attend rather than the online format itself.
He highlights a double standard: online learning must prove itself while face-to-face lecture programs are accepted without comparable evidence.
Treating 'online' as one treatment and lumping very different students into one control group dilutes and confounds the comparison.
Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis shows how strong a hidden confounder would need to be, not whether one exists, so the study's reassurance is overstated.
Regulation aimed at delivery mode risks targeting the wrong problem and burdening non-traditional students who need flexibility.
quotes: Unlike previous research that focuses on individual online courses, OHA examine complete online degree programs. More controversially, they conclude that all such programs require stricter oversight, calling for enhanced regulation from both the Department of Education and accrediting bodies.
Rarely does anyone ask, “Is the classroom any good”. But it’s the first question raised about digital education.

When we see that Group B students complete their degrees at higher rates than Group A students, what are we really measuring? Are we seeing the impact of in-person education, or are we observing the advantages enjoyed by students whose life circumstances allow them to attend traditional classes?

To be clear, this analysis doesn't invalidate OHA's research. However, it suggests an alternative explanation that deserves serious consideration. If the enrollment distribution across institution types accounts for most or all of the observed completion rate gap, then the mode of instruction (online vs. face-to-face) may play a much smaller role, or no role at all, than OHA's conclusions suggest.

Rosenbaum’s method essentially says “Whatever hidden factor(s) might be out there would need to be quite powerful to explain away our results.” But it doesn’t tell us whether such factors do or don’t exist; nor help us identify what the confounders might be; nor rule out the possibility that several confounders working together could have as strong an effect.
This methodological issue has profound implications for policy recommendations. OHA advocates for stricter regulation of online programs based on lower completion rates.
